title: On-demand KV snapshot + priority-based token trimming to avoid GPU OOMs
creator: Maya Chen
description: Summary: We are seeing intermittent OOMs on high-concurrency continuous-batching nodes when long-chat KV caches and large batch sizes coincide. This ticket proposes a multi-pronged recovery and prevention approach: (1) lightweight on-disk KV snapshotting for fast fallback+restore, (2) priority-aware token trimming (drop low-priority prefixes or compress), (3) fast hot-swap to quantized model variants when memory pressure is detected, and (4) a staging layer to preempt low-priority requests instead of OOM-failing them. Goal: reduce OOM incidence to <0.1% of requests in high-KV workloads and bring mean recovery time after an OOM from minutes to <30s.
design_decisions: 1) Snapshot to fast NVMe: periodic incremental snapshots of active KV shards using a TTL window to limit I/O. 2) Token trimming: implement priority-tiered prefix shedding that drops or compresses low-priority assistant/system tokens; maintain token-level provenance for quality auditing. 3) Model downgrade: maintain preloaded quantized model for each major architecture and fast switch-on-pressure rather than cold load post-OOM. 4) Preemption: introduce a 'low-priority queue' with short TTL and early-retry to avoid blocking memory for critical requests.
tradeoffs:
- Snapshotting increases disk I/O and requires coordination across shards; we accept slightly higher IO for faster recovery.
- Token trimming can reduce output fidelity for low-tier traffic; mitigated by preserving high-priority tokens and logging trimmed tokens for later analysis.
- Keeping quantized variants resident uses modest extra memory but avoids long cold-start loads that are worse for user latency.
open_questions:
- How often should snapshots be taken under different workloads? (Every 5s, 30s, adaptive?)
- Should trimming be configurable per-tenant or global?
- How aggressive should automatic model downgrade be vs. explicit routing fallback?
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (spike): implement incremental KV shard snapshot + fast restore shim. Phase 2: add priority token-trimming policy and expose config in routing layer. Phase 3: preload quantized variant and implement hot-swap logic under memory-pressure heuristic. Phase 4: integrate preemption queue and graceful retry/backoff. Phase 5: canary rollout and SLO validation.
test_plan: Unit tests for snapshot/restore correctness, fuzz tests for trimmed-token reconstruction audit logs, load tests with synthetic long-chat workloads (50k concurrent chat sessions), chaos tests simulating node OOM to verify restore and hot-swap within 30s, and A/B tests comparing output quality between downgrades and full models.
monitoring_metrics: OOM-rate, time-to-recover (s), fraction of requests trimmed, fraction of requests downgraded to quantized model, tail-latency P95/P99 under memory-pressure, disk I/O for snapshots, KV-restore failure rate.
rollout: Canary: 5% of serving fleet for 48h with increased logging. If OOMs drop and no regressions in quality metrics, 25% for 24h, then full rollout. Auto-disable if recovery time > 45s or trimmed fraction > 20% for critical customers.
acceptance_criteria: 1) OOM rate <0.1% on benchmark high-KV workload. 2) Recovery time median <15s, 95th <30s. 3) No more than 5% quality regression (BLEU/ROUGE or eval prompts) on sampled traffic for critical customers. 4) No unexpected security exposures from snapshots.
